text:
**Keep the Joins: Why Primary Schools Should Still Teach Joined-Up Handwriting**

Every few years, someone declares handwriting dead. The keyboard has won, the argument goes, and children should spend their scarce classroom hours on coding, or critical thinking, or anything more "relevant" than looping an e on its way to an n. It is a tidy argument. It is also wrong. Primary schools should keep teaching joined-up handwriting, and teach it properly, because it does something for children that nothing else on the timetable does quite as well.

Begin with what the skeptics get right, because they get some of it right. Most adult writing now happens on a screen. Few of us will ever need to produce a page of flowing script under pressure, and the old image of the teacher rapping knuckles over an untidy ascender deserves its retirement. Cursive has no magic. Nobody is a better citizen because their capital G has the right flourish. If joined-up writing were only about looking elegant, I would concede the point and move on.

But it is not only about looking elegant. It is about speed, about memory, and about the strange fact that the hand teaches the mind.

Consider speed first. Print is slow. Each letter requires the pen to lift, travel, and land again, and a child writing in print may lift the pen dozens of times in a single sentence. Joined writing removes most of those lifts. The pen stays on the page; the movement becomes a rhythm rather than a series of stabs. This matters most in exactly the place where handwriting still cannot be avoided: the exam hall. A fluent writer can get their thoughts down before they evaporate. A laboured one cannot. Children who write slowly do not simply finish less; they think less, because the effort of forming letters competes with the effort of composing ideas. Cognitive load is finite. Every ounce a child spends deciding how to shape a letter is an ounce unavailable for deciding what to say.

That is why automaticity is the real prize. Nobody argues that a pianist should keep looking at the keys. The goal of any motor skill is to make it disappear, so that attention is freed for the higher task. Joined-up handwriting, once it is automatic, does this better than print does, because the flow of the movement encodes the spelling. The hand learns that "-ing" is a single gesture, that "th" travels together. Spelling and handwriting reinforce one another. Teachers who work with struggling spellers often notice that children remember a word's shape in their fingers long after they have lost the sequence of its letters in their heads.

There is research behind this, though it deserves honest handling. Studies comparing handwriting with typing, including work by researchers in Norway and the United States using brain imaging, have found that writing by hand activates wider networks than keyboarding does, particularly in young children learning to recognise letters. A well-known experiment found that children who practised letters by hand identified them more readily than those who typed them. Other studies have found that note-taking by hand produces better conceptual understanding than laptop note-taking, since handwriters cannot transcribe everything and must therefore digest and summarise as they go. I would not hang the whole case on any single study; much of this literature is young, and some findings have proved hard to replicate. Still, the direction of travel is consistent. Where researchers have looked, they have rarely found that abandoning handwriting helps.

Now the obvious objection: all of that supports handwriting, not joined-up handwriting. Why not teach print, and be done? Print is easier to learn, easier to read, and closer to the typefaces children see in books.

The reply is that print is not free of cost, and its costs fall later. Children who are taught print and nothing else tend to reach the age of nine or ten and discover that it will not keep up. They start to join letters anyway, on their own, in an improvised and inconsistent way. The result is often worse than if they had been taught: a hybrid scrawl, with joins in odd places and letters that collapse into one another. A taught joined hand, by contrast, is consistent. Its patterns are uniform, so that legibility is a property of the system rather than a matter of luck.

There is also a quieter point about reading. A generation of children who cannot read cursive will be locked out of an enormous amount of the written record. Grandparents' letters. Historical documents. A teacher's marginal comment. The birthday card with a wobbly, loving inscription. Reading handwriting is a literacy skill in its own right, and the surest way to learn it is to produce it. Children who write in cursive can read it. Children who never have often cannot, and the loss is quiet but real. It may sound sentimental to speak of letters from the dead. It is not. It is the practical question of whether a society can read its own papers.

Then there is dyslexia and related difficulties, where the case for joining is, if anything, stronger. Specialist teachers have long favoured cursive for these pupils. Because every letter starts from the same place on the line and flows forward, children are less likely to reverse b and d, and less likely to produce letters that sit loosely and unevenly across the page. Words become units rather than strings of separate marks. This is not a universal rule, and some children with motor difficulties find joining hard. For them, flexibility is right. But as a default for a whole class, a joined hand supports precisely the learners most at risk of falling behind.

What of the claim that time is limited? It is limited. A primary teacher has to deliver reading, mathematics, science, history, music, and a dozen other things, with thirty children and a fixed number of hours. I take this seriously. But handwriting is not a large demand. Short, regular practice, ten minutes several times a week, produces most of the benefit. And since writing is the medium through which children demonstrate nearly everything else they learn, time spent making it fluent is not time taken from other subjects. It is time lent to them, repaid with interest. A child who writes comfortably will write more, and more willingly. A child who dreads the physical act of writing will avoid it, and every subject will suffer.

Nor should we imagine that this is a choice between pens and keyboards. Of course children should learn to type. They should learn it well, and from a sensible age, since keyboard fluency is an essential adult skill. The two are not rivals. A child can master both, much as a child can learn to swim and to cycle. The mistake is to think that because one tool has become more common, the other has become pointless. We still teach children to do arithmetic in their heads, though calculators exist. We still teach them to walk, though cars exist. The argument was never that a skill must be universal to be worth having. It is that certain skills build capacities that carry over.

I will admit that the best defence of cursive is not purely utilitarian. There is something to be said for the satisfaction of it. A child who learns a flowing hand acquires a small, durable craft: a way of making marks that is quick, personal, and theirs. Handwriting is a form of signature. It carries something of the writer, in a way a font never will. We should not make too much of this, but we should not be embarrassed by it either. Education is not only a preparation for employment. It is an introduction to the human inheritance, and writing by hand is a big part of that inheritance.

So what would good practice look like? Teach letter formation early and carefully, in a form that leads naturally into joining. Introduce joins once the shapes are secure, around the age of seven. Keep practice short and frequent. Do not mark children down for imperfect style; mark legibility and fluency. Allow adaptations for those with genuine physical difficulties. And let children develop their own hand, once the foundations are sound, rather than insisting on a rigid model into adulthood.

That is a modest programme. It asks little of schools and gives much back.

The critics are right that the world has changed. They are wrong about what follows. A child who can join letters fluently is faster, spells better, reads more of the past, and carries a skill that frees the mind for harder work. A child who cannot may manage perfectly well, but will have lost something that could have been given cheaply. Schools should not be in the business of withholding useful things from children because the fashion has moved on.

Teach the joins. The pen, it turns out, still has plenty to say.
